items.title: Day 6 Overview — Tasks & Competencies
items.body:
Day 6 · Chapter 5: Tasks, Notes, and Integration

Day 6 Overview

This is the final chapter of the course. Calendar told you when — Tasks is the to-do-list version, and Categories is the color-coding system that ties Mail, Calendar, People, and Tasks together into one workspace. You'll wrap up by seeing how Outlook connects to Word and to your phone.

Competencies Covered Today

  • Work with notes
  • Create and edit tasks
  • Assign and accept/decline tasks
  • Use the Folder list and To-Do bar
  • Integrate Outlook with Word and Excel
  • Access Outlook information on a mobile device

Today's Tasks

  1. Watch the Chapter 5 Presentation
  2. Notes — read, then complete Hands-On OU5-D1
  3. Tasks — read, then complete Hands-On OU5-D2–D4
  4. Categories — read, then complete Hands-On OU5-D5
  5. Integrating with Word and Mobile Devices — read
  6. Chapter 5 Self-Assessment Quiz and Test
Course wrap-up

This is the last day of the Outlook unit — Getting Started → Email → People → Calendar → Tasks/Notes/Integration is one connected workspace, not five separate tools. Business Math begins next class.

items.title: Notes — Reading
items.body:
Day 6 · Chapter 5 Reading

Book page: 84 · Chapter 5 · CBO Objective: Work with notes

Notes

Notes are used to record miscellaneous information you want to save for reference — a short list of reminders, or a quick status note. You access Notes by clicking the three dots in the Navigation bar. Notes are stored in a special Notes folder in Outlook's personal folders. A new note opens as a small box that resembles a yellow sticky note, where you type your text; by default it uses yellow, medium size, and 11-point Calibri, and shows the date/time it was last modified. You must display the Notes view to edit or delete a note.

Notes View

You can look at your notes in one of three standard views: Icon, Notes List, and Last 7 Days. You can customize a view and save it as your own, forward a note to someone or move it to another folder, and categorize notes based on criteria you set.

{{img:pg 84.png|Textbook page 84 — the Notes ribbon showing the Icon/Notes List/Last 7 Days view buttons, Forward/Move/Categorize actions, and a note in Notes List view}}

Copying a Note to the Desktop

A convenient place to display a note is on your computer's Desktop, since you can see it even when Outlook is minimized — just double-click a note to open it in its own Outlook-independent window. The note is still an Outlook item stored in the Notes folder, so editing or deleting it there updates it within Outlook too.

Tip

A note can stay on your Desktop while Outlook is minimized, but closing Outlook closes the note window too — the note itself isn't deleted, it's just no longer displayed until you reopen Outlook and show it again.

items.title: Tasks — Reading
items.body:
Day 6 · Chapter 5 Reading

Book pages: 85-88 · Chapter 5 · CBO Objectives: Create and edit tasks / Assign and accept/decline tasks

Tasks

Tasks appear in your To-Do list and contain due dates. Since many emails you receive require some action, you can quickly flag those emails so they're added to your To-Do list automatically. You can set options for a task like a reminder or a status, assign a task to someone else, and likewise have others assign tasks to you — when you receive one, you can accept or decline it.

{{img:pg 85.png|Textbook page 85 — the Tasks ribbon with Mark Complete, Remove from List, and Flag Task options, and a My Tasks list showing due dates}}

Navigating & Peeking at Tasks

Choose Tasks from the Navigation bar to see your task views; the default is the To-Do list with the Reading pane on the right. Current tasks due also show at the bottom of the Calendar in Day, Week, or Work Week view. Like other Outlook elements, you can peek at your tasks by hovering over the Tasks link on the Navigation bar.

Creating a Task

You can create a task by flagging a message, as a brand-new item, or by dragging an Outlook item onto Tasks on the Navigation bar to create a prepopulated task.

The To-Do Bar

The To-Do bar can display Calendar, People, and/or Tasks, and it's customizable in any Outlook element via View → Layout — useful for keeping track of your calendar and tasks while you're in Mail view, for example.

{{img:pg 86.png|Textbook page 86 — the To-Do bar's task list grouped by No Date, Today, Next Week, and Later}}

Scheduling Calendar Time to Work on a Task

You can drag a task onto your calendar to block out time to work on it. This isn't mandatory, but it helps keep you from over-booking yourself with appointments — the task then follows you on the calendar from day to day as a reminder until you mark it complete, at which point it stays on that day as a record of when you finished it.

Editing Tasks

Tasks are edited in the task view or directly from the To-Do bar — double-clicking opens a separate window where you can change the start/due dates, set a reminder, track status, add a category, or add notes. A task leaves the To-Do list once it's marked complete; the quickest way is clicking its flag icon. The Details view of the To-Do list shows all tasks (complete or in progress), and past-due tasks show in red. A task reminder pops up a notification just like an appointment reminder, and you can Snooze it to be reminded again anywhere from 5 minutes to 2 weeks later.

Assigning and Receiving Tasks

To assign a task to someone else, enter their email address much like inviting someone to a meeting. Once you send it, you're no longer the owner — the recipient is. You can keep a copy in your own task list and ask to be notified when they mark it complete. The recipient can accept or decline; if they accept, you receive an email letting you know (and if they decline, you're notified too).

{{img:pg 88.png|Textbook page 88 — an assigned task in the recipient's Inbox with Accept/Decline buttons, showing who assigned it and its due date}}

When you accept a task assigned to you, the message is removed from your Inbox and the task appears in your task list. Creating a task offers three command options: Mark Complete, Assign Task, and Send Status Report.

items.title: Hands-On OU5-D2–D4: Create, Remind & Assign a Task
items.description:
Book pages: 86-89 · Develop Your Skills OU5-D2 through OU5-D4

Hands-On OU5-D2–D4: Create, Remind & Assign a Task

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — OU5-D2: Create a Task

  1. Click Tasks on the Navigation bar, then choose Home → New Task.
  2. Subject: Set up quarterly training schedule.
  3. Set the Start date to today and the Due date to two weeks from today.
  4. In the detail field, type: Set up training sessions for shelter staff and in-home staff (or your own note).
  5. Click Save & Close.

Part 2 — OU5-D3: Set a Reminder

  1. Double-click your task to reopen it.
  2. Check the Reminder checkbox.
  3. Set the reminder date to one week from today.
  4. Click Save & Close.

Part 3 — OU5-D4: Assign the Task

  1. Double-click your task, then choose Task → Assign Task.
  2. In the To field, enter a classmate's or your instructor's real VACE email address.
  3. Click Send.
What to submit

Three screenshots: (1) the task after Part 1, with its start/due dates and detail note; (2) the task after Part 2, with the Reminder checkbox and date visible; (3) the sent Assign Task window from Part 3, showing your recipient.

items.title: Categories — Reading
items.body:
Day 6 · Chapter 5 Reading

Book pages: 89-91 · Chapter 5

Categories

Categories let you color-code items across every Outlook element — Mail, Calendar, People, Tasks, and Notes — based on criteria you choose. For example, you might create a category for a specific project with its own color to track every email, appointment, contact, task, and note related to it, or simply use colors to separate business items from personal ones.

Once you've created and assigned categories, you can sort by them — in People, for example, you could display every contact color-coded to a specific project. You can also assign a shortcut key to a category to make applying it faster.

{{img:pg 90.png|Textbook page 90 — the Categorize dropdown on the Ribbon, showing Clear All Categories and a list of color-named categories plus All Categories and Set Quick Click options}}

You set and rename categories from the Categorize command, giving each one a name, a color, and (optionally) a shortcut key. Once set up, categories can be applied to any item — an email, a calendar appointment, a contact, a task, or a note — from that same Categorize command on the Ribbon.

{{img:pg 91.png|Textbook page 91 — the Color Categories dialog showing a renamed category, its assigned color, and a shortcut key being set}}

items.title: Hands-On OU5-D5: Set & Assign Categories
items.description:
Book pages: 90-92 · Develop Your Skills OU5-D5

Hands-On OU5-D5: Set & Assign Categories

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — Rename Two Categories

  1. From any Outlook element, choose Home → Categorize → All Categories.
  2. Select the Blue Category, click Rename, and type a project name of your choice.
  3. Click the Shortcut Key button and choose Ctrl+F2.
  4. Select the Green Category, click Rename, and type a second name.
  5. Click the Shortcut Key button and choose Ctrl+F3.
  6. Click OK.

Part 2 — Apply a Category

  1. Go to your Inbox and select any email.
  2. Choose Home → Categorize, then click one of your two renamed categories.
  3. Or: go to your Calendar, select an appointment, and press its category's shortcut key (Ctrl+F2 or Ctrl+F3) instead — notice the appointment changes color.
What to submit

Two screenshots: (1) the Color Categories dialog showing your two renamed categories with their shortcut keys; (2) an email or calendar item with one of your categories applied and visibly color-coded.

items.title: Integrating with Word and Mobile Devices — Reading
items.body:
Day 6 · Chapter 5 Reading

Book pages: 92-93 · Chapter 5 · CBO Objectives: Integrate Outlook with Word and Excel / Access Outlook information on a mobile device

Integrating with Word and Mobile Devices

Outlook works well with other Office applications and with mobile devices, not just on its own.

Creating a Word Mail Merge Using Outlook Contacts

Outlook contacts are organized as a database, which means you can use them elsewhere — exporting to Excel, or performing a mail merge in Word. To bring your Outlook contacts into a Word mail merge, use the Select Recipients → Choose from Outlook Contacts command on Word's Mailings tab. After picking a contact folder, you can check or uncheck which contacts to include in the merge.

{{img:pg 92.png|Textbook page 92 — Word's Select Recipients menu with Choose from Outlook Contacts highlighted, and the Mail Merge Recipients list showing three contacts with checkboxes}}

Working Seamlessly with a Mobile Device

The information you access through Outlook — email, people, calendar, tasks, and notes — can also be accessed on a smartphone or tablet through the free Outlook app (Apple App Store, Google Play, or Microsoft Store). Setting it up uses an Auto Account setup wizard similar to the desktop app. Although your email could be configured in another app on your phone, the Outlook app offers a familiar interface and syncs your email, contacts, appointments, and tasks — even reminders display on your device.

{{img:pg 93.png|Textbook page 93 — three mobile phone screens: the Outlook app's Add Account setup screen, the sign-in screen, and a synced Inbox}}
Note for this course

The CBO objective for this topic covers integrating with both Word and Excel, but the textbook itself only details the Word mail-merge process above (it mentions exporting contacts to Excel in passing, with no dedicated walkthrough). There's no separate Hands-On for Excel integration today for that reason.

On the C: drive of the computer

questions.question_text: Where are tasks displayed?
Match each task option to its description.

matches.right: Create and send a task to a contact, who accepts or declines it
An alert that prompts you to work on a task
Indication of progress made or the current state of a task

questions.question_text: Which of these is NOT a way to create a task?

answers.text: Use the Type a New Task box.
Drag an item to Tasks on the Navigation bar.

questions.question_text: What is an easy way to schedule calendar time to work on a task?

answers.text: Export the task from the To-Do Bar to the day before the due date.
Right-click the task in the Navigation bar peek and choose Remind.
Drag the task onto the calendar so it travels from day to day until you mark it as complete.
Set up a series of appointments with action items related to the task.

questions.question_text: Match each task view type to its description.

matches.right: The default, this view displays the Reading pane to its right.
Keeps your task list visible while you work in another Outlook element

questions.question_text: How is the start date for a task determined?

answers.text: The task originator/creator specifies it during creation.
It's always the date the task is created.
This is done according to when the person assigned the task accepts it.
By default, the start date is always one day after the task is created.

questions.question_text: What happens when you send a task to someone?

answers.text: It appears on the recipient's calendar at the start and due dates.
You remain the task owner until the recipient responds to the task.
The recipient receives the task and can then accept or decline it.
The Manage Task bar appears on the Navigation bar for you and the recipient.

questions.question_text: When does a task recipient become the task owner?

answers.text: As soon as the originator sends it

questions.question_text: What happens when you accept a task from someone else?

answers.text: The calendar opens so you can indicate the due date and set a reminder.
The message is removed from your Inbox and the task appears in your task list.
Outlook prompts you to set up the status report schedule.
The task is highlighted on the To-Do bar until you mark it complete.

questions.question_text: What is an advantage of the To-Do bar?

answers.text: The categories it sets by default can be customized, or you can create rules.
It automatically blocks out time on your calendar for you to work on tasks.
The contextual Ribbon tab appears with more options when you turn on the To-Do bar.
It's customizable and can show in any of the Outlook elements, helping you keep track of tasks, calendar items, and contacts.

questions.question_text: What can you do to organize tasks in your To-Do list when you have many tasks that deal with the same project or topic?

answers.text: Create folders for tasks associated with the different projects.
Start declining tasks to ensure you don't get overloaded.
Use different flag colors for different projects.

questions.question_text: To create a mail merge, you can _____ your Outlook contacts into Word.

What information that you access through Outlook can you also access on a mobile device?
Why use the Outlook app rather than, for example, the email app associated with your smartphone?

answers.text: It's the only way to access your Outlook information on a mobile device.
The app syncs your email, contacts, appointments, and tasks.
